profile.campus: Csquare Silicon Valley campus cluster (SFO1-SFO4, formerly Centersquare, formerly Evoque Data Center Solutions)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
This building sits at 2401 Walsh Avenue in Santa Clara, California, roughly 370 feet north of the 2403 Walsh Avenue building that, together with this one, makes up Csquare's SFO1 site. Geocoding 2401 Walsh Avenue lands within about 40 feet of this record's stored coordinates. The City of Santa Clara parcel layer returns assessor parcel 216-28-127 here, zoned LI for light industrial, general plan light industrial, in Council District 1, with a construction year of 1997, a full generation newer than the 1973 shell next door at 2403 Walsh, which this registry also carries as a separate record.

Csquare's own SEC registration prospectus splits the SFO1 code into two rentable units rather than treating it as one building, SFO1_A at 60,982 rentable square feet, 64.9 percent occupied as of March 31, 2026, and SFO1_B at 38,634 rentable square feet, 63.9 percent occupied, both company owned. Which suffix corresponds to this 1997 building versus its 1973 neighbor could not be confirmed this session, so no individual floor area or occupancy figure is written to this record. Csquare's facility page for SFO1 as a whole, both buildings combined, states 95,981 square feet of raised floor, 34.5 megawatts of utility power, 11.2 megawatts of UPS protected capacity, and 17.5 megawatts of generator capacity, certified to SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS, NIST 800-53 PE High, and ISO 27001 standards plus ENERGY STAR, with nine carrier neutral service providers on site. Those figures describe the SFO1 pair together rather than this building alone.

Csquare, Inc., trading on the New York Stock Exchange as CSQR, reports having begun operations in January 2019 under the name BIF III US Aggregator (Delaware) LLC, a corporate lineage that continued through Evoque Data Center Solutions under Brookfield affiliated ownership, then Centersquare, then Csquare, converting to a Delaware corporation on June 15, 2026 shortly before a July 16, 2026 initial public offering priced at 21 dollars a share across 50 million shares for roughly 1.05 billion dollars gross. Brookfield Corporation retained approximately 69 percent of voting power afterward, making Csquare a controlled company under New York Stock Exchange rules. As of March 31, 2026 the company's portfolio spanned 64 sites across 21 metro markets in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, totaling roughly 389 megawatts of sellable power capacity and more than 1,700 customers, and its own prospectus names California, alongside Boston, as a market where power costs run higher and more volatile than the company average, a caution this Santa Clara building sits squarely inside.

Silicon Valley Power, the City of Santa Clara's municipal electric utility, reported a peak demand of 746.5 megawatts across 62,447 electric accounts as of its December 2025 fact sheet and stated that more than fifty data centers in the city account for 53 percent of the utility's power sales, a concentration that led the utility's chief operating officer to tell San Jose Spotlight in May 2025 that operators had already requested 500 additional megawatts of load against a peak near 720, prompting the city to cap new data center approvals while grid expansion work is projected to run through 2029. No tenant is named for either SFO1 unit in any source reviewed.

reading.body:
This building is one of two at Csquare's SFO1 campus in Santa Clara, part of a two-building pair reporting 34.5 megawatts of utility power and 11.2 megawatts of UPS-protected capacity together. The pair holds 95,981 square feet of raised floor across both units at occupancies near 64 percent as of March 2026. Certifications qualify the campus for SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type II workloads, PCI DSS compliance, NIST 800-53 PE High security, and ISO 27001 data handling.

At a typical AI training density of 40 kilowatts per rack, the 34.5 megawatts of utility power available across both SFO1 buildings would support roughly 860 racks, assuming IT load runs at 70 percent of utility power after overhead. The exact split between this 1997 building and its 1973 neighbor is not published. No tenant is named for either SFO1 unit in public sources.

Santa Clara sits in a constrained power market where data centers already consume 53 percent of municipal utility sales and operators have requested 500 additional megawatts against a peak near 720 megawatts, prompting the city to cap new approvals while grid work runs through 2029. This campus ranks 12th among the 11 facilities with published megawatt figures in California, a state where this site has mapped 103 data center locations but only one of nine has made capacity public. California's published total across mapped sites stands at 365 megawatts, placing Santa Clara near the frontier of constraint rather than surplus.
